items.abstract: <jats:p>Tool-calling LLM agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection: externally retrieved data can redirect tool calls without system-prompt access, and prompt-level defences leave three harm classes undefended (path traversal, user-guided exfiltration, high-frequency tool abuse). We present a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) that intercepts at the tool-call boundary with declarative rules over a cross-step information-flow label system (source integrity, data sensitivity) and a synchronous SHA-256 hash-chained audit log. On a controlled dataset across four attack classes, the full system cuts the attack success rate (ASR) from 40.0% to 5.0% (deepseek-v4-pro, five repeats) versus 35.0% for the strongest prompt-only baseline; disabling cross-step label propagation raises the call-level false-negative rate by 26.4 points. The 30.0% task-level false-positive rate is dominated by by-design least-privilege capability-token denials, not rule false positives—an expanded 30-task benign set yields 0/30 rule false positives under scripted isolation. A conservative-DS mitigation (intent-taint) closes the constructed denied-read reconstruction blind-spot variant (ASR 100% to 0%) at no cost on standard workflows. The audit log detects all three tested tamper classes; the in-process enforcement overhead is sub-millisecond per call. Across four further backends, ASR drops under the full system, though LLaMA-3.3-70B retains 16.7% (a rule-coverage gap). A preliminary run over a real MCP stdio transport (an official filesystem server) shows the mechanism operates at a real boundary with a sub-millisecond execution-path increment. We frame these as mechanism-coverage evidence on a controlled benchmark, not a deployability claim for production MCP workloads. Code, data, and metrics are openly available in the replication repository.</jats:p>
title: Runtime Policy Enforcement for MCP-Based LLM Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>We design a lightweight runtime monitor that enforces API-call policies for programs generated by large language models. The monitor uses syscall tracing and taint propagation to detect forbidden behavior, including unsafe file access, insecure crypto choices, and untrusted deserialization. Evaluations on 400 LLM-generated programs show that runtime enforcement blocks 92% of dangerous behaviors without requiring code modification. Performance overhead remains below 7% on average. Complementing static or pre-generation safeguards, runtime policy enforcement offers a robust last line of defense.</jats:p>
title: Runtime Policy Enforcement for Mitigating Risks in LLM-Generated Programs Authors

items.abstract: <jats:p>Desktop LLM agents that invoke tools fail in mundane but costly ways: large tool catalogs inflate prompts, the same tool-specific errors recur across sessions, and long conversations can lose tool-call/result pairing during compression. WeClaw, an open-source and deployed adaptive runtime for desktop agents, treats these failures as software-reliability problems rather than isolated prompting mistakes. It combines Progressive Tool Exposure with Failure-Driven Escalation (PTE-FD), Event-Based Experience Auto-Capture (EBEAC), and a Robust Context Pipeline (RCR). PTE-FD first exposes about ten recommended tools and broadens the set only after observable execution failures. EBEAC records failure patterns from the runtime event bus without extra LLM calls. RCR preserves the structural contract between assistant tool calls and tool results before context pruning. We evaluated PTE-FD across four OpenAI-compatible back-ends (deepseek-v4-flash, qwen-max, moonshot-v1-8k, and glm-4-flash), using three seeds per model and N=288 pooled matched outcomes per model. PTE-FD achieved the highest tool-selection accuracy for every back-end, significantly outperforming full static exposure (Holm-Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.001) and plain tiered exposure (Holm-corrected p < 0.05), while reducing tool-schema tokens by 46-57%. The broader evaluation includes a bilingual 500-query rerun, a faithful instruction-tool retrieval reproduction, RCR compression tests, EBEAC replay experiments, and a 30-day production snapshot of 1,210 sessions. The results suggest that modest runtime mechanisms, released as a reproducible open-source system, can improve reliability when tool-augmented agents move from demonstrations to daily desktop use.​</jats:p>
title: WeClaw: An Open-Source Adaptive Runtime Framework for Tool-Augmented Desktop LLM Agents
